antiBlank.title: THE ADHD ANTI-BLANK PROTOCOL & TECHNICAL INTERVIEW EXECUTION MANUAL
headers: EXACT SCRIPT / PHYSICAL ACTION (EXTERNALIZE WORKING MEMORY)
rows: 1. WHY YOU BLANK OUT AFTER 100+ QUESTIONS (ADHD ROOT CAUSE)
Working Memory Bottleneck

When you read a 3-paragraph LeetCode prompt, your brain tries to hold the story, constraints, examples, edge cases, AND search through 100+ past problems inside your head all at once. For an ADHD brain, this instantly overflows working memory — triggering a protective 'freeze / blank screen' response.
RULE #1: Never think in your head. If your hands are not typing/writing within 5 seconds of reading the first sentence, your working memory is overloading.
1. WHY YOU BLANK OUT AFTER 100+ QUESTIONS (ADHD ROOT CAUSE)
Episodic vs. Trigger Memory

Solving 100+ problems by reading the problem -> coding -> submitting stores 'episodic memory' (how that specific solution looked), NOT 'trigger memory' (what cue in the question points to what tool). When a new question wears a different costume, episodic memory fails.
RULE #2: Strip the story costume immediately. Every problem is just: Input Type + Constraint (N) + Goal Verb.
2. THE 90-SECOND ADHD 'UN-FREEZE' RITUAL (DO THIS ON EVERY QUESTION)
Second 0–20: The Costume Stripper
Do NOT read the whole problem twice. On your very first read, type 3 lines in the code editor comment box to dump the problem out of your head:

# INPUT: nums (unsorted int array), k (int)
# OUTPUT: max length of contiguous subarray with sum == k
# N_SIZE: N <= 2 * 10^5 (means O(N^2) is TLE! Must be O(N) or O(N log N))
2. THE 90-SECOND ADHD 'UN-FREEZE' RITUAL (DO THIS ON EVERY QUESTION)
Second 20–50: Manual Hand-Trace on 1 Tiny Example
Your brain cannot invent an algorithm in the abstract, but it CAN watch what your hands do on a 4-element example. Trace Example 1 by hand and ask: 'What did my eyes just look back at?'

# Example: nums = [1, 2, 3, -2, 5], k = 5
# At index 2 (sum=6), my eyes looked back to see if I ever had sum = 6 - 5 = 1!
# 'Looking back for a past value in O(1)' = HASHMAP!
2. THE 90-SECOND ADHD 'UN-FREEZE' RITUAL (DO THIS ON EVERY QUESTION)
Second 50–90: The 5-Bucket Elimination Checklist
Instead of searching 500 problems in your head, run down this fixed 5-item checklist written at the top of your scratchpad:

1. Is it contiguous subarray/substring? -> Sliding Window (if positive) OR Prefix Sum + HashMap (if negatives)
2. Is it sorted or 'min max / max min'? -> Two Pointers OR Binary Search on Answer
3. Do I need Next Greater/Smaller or Top K? -> Monotonic Stack OR Heap
4. Is it connections/grid/dependencies? -> BFS (shortest) / DFS / Topo Sort / Union-Find
5. Is it 'count all ways' or 'min/max choices'? -> DP (memoize recursion) OR Backtracking (if N <= 20)
3. HOW TO SOLVE A QUESTION IN A LIVE 45-MIN INTERVIEW
Min 0–3: Clarify & Strip (UMPIRE - Understand)
Read/listen, write down Input/Output/Constraints on the shared pad, and ask 2 targeted edge-case questions (this buys your brain calm processing time!).
Say out loud: 'Just to make sure I have the constraints right: can the array contain negative numbers or duplicates? And what is the max size of N?'
3. HOW TO SOLVE A QUESTION IN A LIVE 45-MIN INTERVIEW
Min 3–8: Brute Force Out Loud First (Drop the Perfectionism)

ADHD brains freeze because they try to jump straight to the clever O(N) trick. State the dumb O(N^2) or O(2^N) brute force in 2 sentences FIRST. It unlocks your brain and gets partial credit immediately.
Say out loud: 'The naive approach is checking every pair (i, j), which takes O(N^2) time and O(1) space. Notice that the bottleneck is repeatedly scanning for X...'
3. HOW TO SOLVE A QUESTION IN A LIVE 45-MIN INTERVIEW
Min 8–14: Optimize the Bottleneck & Write Skeleton Comments
Identify the repeated work in the brute force and swap in the DSA element that fixes it. BEFORE writing real code, write 4 lines of plain-English comments inside the function.

# 1. Initialize HashMap {0: -1} and running_sum = 0
# 2. Loop i, num in enumerate(nums)
# 3. Check if (running_sum - k) is in HashMap -> update max_len
# 4. Store running_sum in HashMap if not present
3. HOW TO SOLVE A QUESTION IN A LIVE 45-MIN INTERVIEW
Min 14–32: Fill in the Skeleton (Breadcrumb Coding)
Now your ADHD brain only has to translate 1 comment line at a time into code! If you get interrupted or lose your train of thought, your comments tell you exactly where you are.
Never delete your skeleton comments while coding — write the code directly underneath each comment step.
3. HOW TO SOLVE A QUESTION IN A LIVE 45-MIN INTERVIEW
Min 32–40: Dry Run with a State Table & State Complexity
Do NOT just read your code and say 'looks good'. Create a 1-line comment tracker for your variables (`i=0, sum=1, ans=0`) and step through 1 small example and 1 edge case (empty/single element).
Finish with: 'Time complexity is O(N) because we visit each element once with O(1) HashMap lookups, and Space is O(N) for the HashMap.'
4. HOW TO PRACTICE LEETCODE LIKE A REAL INTERVIEW SCENARIO
Rule 1: Never Code Silent & Never Hit 'Run Code' Early
On LeetCode, spamming the 'Run' button every 2 minutes trains trial-and-error coding, which causes panic in real interviews where code execution is disabled or judged.
Speak out loud (even to a rubber duck or voice memo) while solving. You are only allowed to click 'Run' AFTER you have dry-run your code manually on a test case in comments.
4. HOW TO PRACTICE LEETCODE LIKE A REAL INTERVIEW SCENARIO
Rule 2: The 20-Minute Hard Stop (Prevent ADHD Hyperfocus Burnout)
Spending 90 minutes stuck on 1 problem drains all your dopamine for the day. Use a strict 20-minute timer for planning + coding.

At Minute 10: If still blank, read ONLY the 'ADHD Anti-Blank Trigger' column in Tab 1.
At Minute 20: If not solved, read the editorial/solution concept (NOT the code), close the solution, and code it yourself from memory.
Then mark it in Tab 1 so the 7-Day Review Queue tests you cold next week!

decoder.title: HOW TO RECOGNIZE PATTERNS JUST BY READING THE QUESTION (CONSTRAINTS + KEYWORDS DECODER)
headers: WHAT YOU SEE IN THE QUESTION / CONSTRAINTS
rows: 1. INPUT SIZE (N) DECODER
O(2^N) or O(N!)
Backtracking OR Bitmask DP
Exponential is allowed! Whenever N <= 20, the interviewer WANTS you to try all subsets/permutations or represent visited state as an integer bitmask.
1. INPUT SIZE (N) DECODER
O(N^3) or O(N^2)
Interval DP / Floyd-Warshall / 2D DP
Small enough for nested loops over (i, j, k) intervals or all-pairs shortest path.
1. INPUT SIZE (N) DECODER
2D DP Table dp[i][j] / Nested Two Pointers (like 3Sum)
10^6 operations easily pass in 1 second. Think 2D grid/string table or fixing one element + Two Pointers.
1. INPUT SIZE (N) DECODER
O(N log N) or O(N)
Sorting + Two Pointers, Heap, Binary Search, Sliding Window, Prefix Sum + HashMap, Monotonic Stack, BFS/DFS
O(N^2) will 100% Time Limit Exceed (TLE)! You MUST eliminate the inner loop using a HashMap, Two Pointers, Monotonic Stack, Heap, or Binary Search.
1. INPUT SIZE (N) DECODER
O(log N) or O(1)
Binary Search on Answer / Math / Bitwise / Matrix Exponentiation
You cannot even loop from 1 to N! You must halve the search space every step.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Contiguous subarray / substring' + 'Max/Min/Longest' + All Positive Numbers
O(N)
Sliding Window (Expand Right, Shrink Left)
Because numbers are positive, expanding R always increases the sum and shrinking L always decreases it (monotonic window property).
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Contiguous subarray' + 'Sum equals K / divisible by K' + NEGATIVE Numbers Allowed
O(N)
Prefix Sum + HashMap {prefix_sum: count_or_first_idx}
Negatives break Sliding Window! Prefix sum turns subarray sum(i..j) into prefix[j] - prefix[i-1] == K, which is just Two Sum on prefix sums.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Sorted array' + 'Pair / Triplet sum' OR 'In-place remove duplicates'
O(N) or O(N^2)
Two Pointers (Left & Right moving inward, or Slow & Fast)
Sorting gives directional certainty: if sum < target, move Left++; if sum > target, move Right--.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Next greater element', 'Days until warmer', 'Largest rectangle in histogram'
O(N)
Monotonic Stack (storing indices)
Whenever you scan an array and need the first element to the left/right that is larger or smaller than current, a Monotonic Stack resolves all waiting elements in O(1) amortized.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Maximum/minimum in every sliding window of size K'
O(N)
Monotonic Deque (Double-Ended Queue)
Pop smaller elements from the back (they can never be the max) and pop expired indices (< R - K + 1) from the front.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Minimize the maximum' OR 'Maximize the minimum' (e.g., ship capacity, Koko bananas, split array)
O(N log(Range))
Binary Search on Answer (Parametric Search)
Whenever you can easily write a greedy function `canWeDoItWith(X)` in O(N), and if X works then X+1 also works, binary search on X!
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Top K frequent', 'Kth largest', 'K closest', 'Merge K sorted'
O(N log K)
Heap / Priority Queue (Min-Heap of size K)
Any time you maintain the best K items dynamically without sorting the entire N-element array.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Running median' OR 'Balance two halves dynamically'
O(log N) per insert
Two Heaps (Max-Heap for lower half + Min-Heap for upper half)
Max-Heap gives O(1) access to the largest of the small numbers; Min-Heap gives O(1) access to the smallest of the large numbers.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Shortest path / minimum steps' in an unweighted grid, maze, or word transformation
O(V + E)
Breadth-First Search (BFS) / Multi-Source BFS
BFS explores distance 1, then distance 2, then distance 3 — the first time it hits the target is guaranteed to be the shortest path.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Prerequisites', 'Course schedule', 'Build order', 'Dependencies'
O(V + E)
Topological Sort (Kahn's Indegree Queue or DFS Cycle Detection)
Dependencies form a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Start with nodes that have 0 prerequisites (in-degree == 0).
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Connected components', 'Redundant connection', 'Accounts merge', 'Dynamic grouping'
O(N * alpha(N))
Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union - DSU)
Whenever edges arrive one by one and you need to check if two nodes are already in the same group or merge two groups in O(1).
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Number of ways to...', 'Min cost to reach...', 'Longest subsequence', 'Can we partition...'
O(N * Target) or O(N^2)
Dynamic Programming (Top-Down Memoization or Bottom-Up Table)
You have overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure — you don't need to print all actual combinations, just the count/max/min.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Generate ALL valid combinations / permutations / subsets / board configurations'
O(2^N) or O(N!)
Backtracking (Choose -> Explore -> Unchoose)
Because the question asks you to return the actual list of all valid configurations, you MUST explicitly build and backtrack every valid path.
2. PROMPT KEYWORD DECODER
'Prefix match', 'Autocomplete', 'Dictionary word search on 2D board'
O(L) per word
Trie (Prefix Tree)
Sharing character prefixes across thousands of words avoids repeating string comparisons from scratch.

linker.title: HOW TO KNOW WHAT DSA ELEMENTS TO USE & HOW TO LINK THEM TOGETHER (LEGO ARCHITECTURE)
rows: 1. HashMap + Doubly Linked List
HashMap: Gives O(1) lookup by key, but has NO idea of order or recency.
Doubly Linked List: Maintains order & allows O(1) node removal/insertion at head/tail if you already have the node pointer, but takes O(N) to find a node.
Store the Linked List Node object as the VALUE inside the HashMap: `map[key] = Node(key, val)`. Lookup in O(1) via Map -> splice & move Node to head in O(1) via DLL pointers!
Q109 / Q472: LRU Cache, Q110 / Q473: LFU Cache, Q502: All O'one Data Structure
2. HashMap + Dynamic Array (List)
HashMap: O(1) insert, O(1) delete, O(1) lookup, but CANNOT pick a random element in O(1) (no index addressing).
Dynamic Array (List): O(1) `random.choice(arr)` by index, and O(1) append/pop at the VERY END, but O(N) to find or delete from the middle.
Store `map[val] = index_in_array`. To delete `val` in O(1): look up its index `i = map[val]`, overwrite `arr[i] = arr[-1]` (the last element), update `map[arr[-1]] = i`, and `arr.pop()`!
Q486: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1), Q487: Duplicates Allowed
3. Prefix Sum + HashMap
Prefix Sum: Computes `sum(i..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]` in O(1), but finding which past `i` gives a sum of K still takes an O(N) loop.
HashMap: Stores `{past_prefix_sum: count_or_earliest_index}` so you can ask 'Have I seen `curr_sum - K` before?' in O(1).
As you loop once through the array, maintain `curr_sum += num`, check `if (curr_sum - k) in seen_map`, then update `seen_map[curr_sum]`.
Q21: Subarray Sum Equals K, Q23: Continuous Subarray Sum, Q26: Contiguous Array (0s & 1s)
4. Sliding Window + HashMap / Counter
Two Pointers (L, R): Define a contiguous window `s[L..R]`, but don't know if the characters inside the window satisfy the constraint.
HashMap / Counter + `matched` integer: Tracks exact frequencies inside `[L..R]` and how many unique required characters are currently satisfied.
Expand `R` -> add `s[R]` to Counter (if count hits target, `matched += 1`). While `matched == required`: update best answer and shrink `L` (`s[L]` leaves Counter).
Q11: Longest Substring Without Repeating, Q14: Minimum Window Substring, Q17: Find All Anagrams
5. Monotonic Stack + Original Array
Array: Stores heights/temperatures by index, but finding the next greater or smaller element takes O(N) per element.
Stack of Indices: Keeps indices whose values are in strictly monotonic order (waiting for their 'Next Greater/Smaller' match).
Push INDEX `i` (not just value!) onto the stack. When `nums[i] > nums[stack[-1]]`, pop `prev_idx = stack.pop()`; the distance is `i - prev_idx` and value is `nums[prev_idx]`.
Q121: Daily Temperatures, Q122: Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Q84: Remove K Digits
6. Two Heaps (Max-Heap + Min-Heap)
Single Heap: Can only give you the global minimum OR global maximum in O(1), not the middle (median) element.
Max-Heap (`left_half`) + Min-Heap (`right_half`): Splits the sorted stream at the exact midpoint so both middle elements sit at the tops of the two heaps!
Push new number to `left_half` (negated for Max-Heap in Python), pop its largest into `right_half`, and if `len(right) > len(left)`, pop back to `left`. Median is `left[0]` or average of tops!
Q241: Find Median from Data Stream, Q242: Sliding Window Median, Q243: IPO
7. Trie (Prefix Tree) + DFS Backtracking
DFS on 2D Grid: Explores paths on a board, but checking 10,000 dictionary words separately takes 10,000 * O(4^L) time.
Trie: Compresses all 10,000 dictionary words into a single prefix tree so one single DFS explores all words simultaneously.
Pass `curr_trie_node` directly as a parameter into `dfs(r, c, trie_node)`. If `board[r][c]` is not in `trie_node.children`, PRUNE immediately in O(1)!
Q226: Word Search II, Q478: Design Search Autocomplete System
8. Binary Search + Greedy Helper Function
Greedy Scan: Can easily verify 'Is capacity X enough to ship in D days?' in O(N), but doesn't know the minimum X.
Binary Search: Searches the monotonic answer range `[min_possible, max_possible]` in O(log(Range)) steps.
Write `def feasible(mid): ...` first. Then run `while lo < hi: mid = (lo+hi)//2; if feasible(mid): hi = mid else: lo = mid + 1`.
Q154: Capacity to Ship Packages, Q155: Split Array Largest Sum, Q156: Koko Eating Bananas
9. Adjacency List + In-Degree Array + BFS Queue
Adjacency List `graph[u] = [v1, v2]`: Shows who depends on `u`, but doesn't tell you which nodes have 0 unmet prerequisites right now.
In-Degree Array `indeg[v]` + Queue: Tracks how many prerequisites each node has left, and queues nodes as soon as `indeg[v] == 0`.
Build `graph` and `indeg`. Push all `u` with `indeg[u] == 0` to `deque`. Pop `u`, append to result, and for `v` in `graph[u]`: `indeg[v] -= 1; if indeg[v] == 0: queue.append(v)`.
Q269: Course Schedule, Q270: Course Schedule II, Q278: Alien Dictionary
10. Adjacency List + Min-Heap + Distance Array
BFS Queue: Only works when all edge weights are equal (1). Fails on weighted graphs.
Min-Heap Priority Queue `[(cost, u)]` + `dist[u]` Array: Always expands the cheapest reachable node next (Dijkstra's Algorithm).
Pop `(d, u)` from Min-Heap. If `d > dist[u]: continue` (skip stale heap entry!). For `(v, weight)` in `graph[u]`: if `d + weight < dist[v]`, update `dist[v]` and `heappush`.
Q292: Network Delay Time, Q296: Path with Minimum Effort, Q288: Swim in Rising Water
11. Sorting + Union-Find (DSU)
Union-Find: Merges components and checks connectivity in O(1), but doesn't know what order to process edges/queries.
Sorting Edges/Queries by Weight: Ensures we greedily connect the cheapest edges first (Kruskal's MST) or process threshold queries monotonically.
Sort `edges` by weight ascending. Loop `(w, u, v)`: if `union(u, v)` returns `True` (they weren't connected yet), add `w` to `total_cost`.
Q302: Min Cost to Connect All Points, Q274: Accounts Merge, Q291: Remove Max Number of Edges
12. Recursion (DFS) + Memoization HashMap/Table
Recursion (Backtracking): Easy to express choices (`take` vs `skip`), but recomputes the exact same `(index, remaining_target)` state millions of times.
Memoization Cache `memo[(i, state)]` (or `@lru_cache(None)`): Turns an O(2^N) decision tree into an O(N * State) Dynamic Programming solution in 1 line of code!
Identify the changing parameters of `dfs(i, state)`. Before computing, check `if (i, state) in memo: return memo[(i, state)]`. Store result before returning.
Q314: Coin Change, Q328: Longest Common Subsequence, Q340: Target Sum, Q359: Stock with Cooldown
